name: Egyptian Koshari
description: Koshari, Egypt's national dish, is genuinely a layered combination of rice, lentils, pasta, and vermicelli, topped with a cooked spicy tomato sauce, a separate uncooked garlic-vinegar sauce, and real crispy fried onions - it's not one component pretending to be several, it's actually this many parts, and shortcutting any of them misses the dish entirely.

steps_detailed: Toss the sliced onion with the flour and fry in the oil until deeply golden and crisp, 8-10 minutes. Drain on paper towels.
Cook the rice and lentils together in salted water until both are tender, about 20 minutes.
Cook the ditalini per package directions. Toast the broken vermicelli in a dry pan until golden, then cook briefly in water until tender.
For the tomato sauce: simmer the tomatoes with half the garlic and half the cumin for 15 minutes until thickened.
For the garlic-vinegar sauce (da'ah): whisk the remaining garlic, vinegar, remaining cumin, and a splash of water together - this sauce is never cooked.
Layer the rice-lentil mixture, pasta, vermicelli, and chickpeas in a bowl. Top with the tomato sauce, a drizzle of the garlic-vinegar sauce, and the crispy onions.

name: Egyptian Ful Medames
description: Ful medames, slow-simmered fava beans mashed with garlic, lemon, and oil, is one of Egypt's oldest and most essential dishes, eaten at nearly any meal, especially breakfast - real versions leave the beans a little rustic and textured rather than pureed completely smooth, and a scatter of chopped tomato and a soft-boiled egg on top is genuine, common practice, not a modern add-on.
steps_detailed: Simmer the fava beans with a splash of water, 8-10 minutes, until very soft.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving real texture rather than pureeing smooth, and stir in the garlic, lemon juice, cumin, and half the olive oil.
Spoon into a bowl, top with the diced tomato, and drizzle with the remaining olive oil before serving.

name: Egyptian Ta'ameya
description: Ta'ameya, Egypt's real ancestor of falafel, is made from fava beans rather than chickpeas - this is the genuine, original version, not a variation, and the fava beans give it a greener interior and softer bite than the chickpea falafel found elsewhere in the region.
steps_detailed: Blend the fava beans, garlic, cilantro, and mint into a coarse, thick paste.
Shape into small patties and press sesame seeds onto the outside.
Fry, turning, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply golden and crisp outside.

name: Egyptian Molokhia
description: Molokhia, a garlicky, herbaceous green soup, is one of Egypt's most beloved traditional dishes - real molokhia leaf isn't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in, though it lacks the real dish's distinctive silky, slightly mucilaginous texture that gives molokhia its character.
steps_detailed: Simmer the chicken in the broth 20-22 minutes until tender, then remove and shred, reserving the broth.
Blend the spinach until finely chopped.
Cook the garlic and coriander in a little oil 1 minute until fragrant, then add the spinach and reserved broth.
Simmer 10-12 minutes, then return the shredded chicken.
steps: Simmer the chicken in the broth 20-22 minutes until tender, then remove and shred, reserving the broth.
Blend the spinach until finely chopped.
Cook the garlic and coriander in a little oil 1 minute until fragrant, then add the spinach and reserved broth.
Simmer 10-12 minutes, then return the shredded chicken.

name: Egyptian Dukkah
description: Dukkah, a toasted nut, seed, and spice blend, is a real Egyptian condiment made completely from scratch - roasting the hazelnuts and toasting the sesame seeds and coriander separately before grinding is what gives it real depth, not a shortcut of just mixing ground spices together.
steps_detailed: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan until fragrant and the skins loosen, 5-6 minutes, then rub off the skins.
Toast the sesame seeds and coriander separately, each until fragrant, 2-3 minutes.
Coarsely grind everything together with the cumin and pepper - dukkah should stay coarse and textured, not become a powder.

name: Egyptian Shorbat Ads
description: Shorbat ads, a smooth, cumin-forward red lentil soup, is a beloved everyday Egyptian dish, real versions finished with a real garlic-cumin oil drizzled on top right at the table, not stirred in early, so its aroma stays bright.
steps_detailed: Simmer the lentils, onion, and carrot in 2.5 cups water 20-22 minutes until completely soft.
Blend until smooth.
Cook the garlic and cumin in the olive oil 30 seconds until fragrant.
Stir the lemon juice into the soup, then drizzle the garlic-cumin oil over each bowl right before serving.

name: Egyptian Fattah
description: Fattah, layered toasted bread, rice, and a garlicky vinegar-tomato sauce, is a real Egyptian celebration dish, traditionally made for Eid and other special occasions - the bread stays at the bottom of the dish, meant to soak up the sauce, not served on the side.

ingredients_full.ingredient: 365 (Whole Foods) 365 Everyday Value, White Hamburger Buns

steps_detailed: Cook the rice separately.
Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.
Simmer the garlic, vinegar, and tomatoes together 10 minutes into a tangy sauce.
Layer the toasted bread at the bottom of a serving dish, top with the rice, then the beef, then the sauce.

name: Egyptian Mahshi (Stuffed Cabbage)
description: Mahshi, cabbage leaves stuffed with rice and herbs, is a genuine Egyptian home-cooking staple, traditionally rolled tightly and thin by hand into small cylinders - real technique lining the pot with extra cabbage leaves or tomato slices first so the rolls don't scorch on the bottom during the long simmer.

ingredients_full.note: leaves separated, a few extra reserved for lining the pot

ingredients.note: leaves separated, a few extra reserved for lining the pot

steps_detailed: Blanch the cabbage leaves 2-3 minutes until pliable.
Mix the raw rice with half the tomatoes, the cilantro, mint, and garlic.
Roll a spoonful of the filling tightly into each cabbage leaf, tucking in the sides as you go.
Line the bottom of a pot with a few extra cabbage leaves to prevent scorching, then arrange the rolls snugly in the pot.
Cover with the remaining tomatoes, lemon juice, and enough water to just cover, and simmer 30-35 minutes until the rice is tender.

name: Egyptian Shakshuka
description: Shakshuka, eggs poached in a spiced tomato sauce, is beloved across Egypt and the wider region, a common breakfast or light dinner, real technique building a genuinely thick sauce first so the eggs poach gently rather than boil.
steps_detailed: Cook the bell pepper and garlic in the olive oil 3-4 minutes until softened.
Add the tomatoes and cumin, and simmer 10-12 minutes into a thick sauce.
Make wells in the sauce and crack the eggs in.
Cover and cook 5-6 minutes until the whites are set but the yolks stay soft.

name: Egyptian Baba Ghanoush
description: Baba ghanoush, a smoky roasted eggplant dip, real depth coming from genuinely charring the eggplant until the skin blackens, not just baking it soft.
steps_detailed: Char the whole eggplant directly over a flame or under a broiler, turning occasionally, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and the flesh is completely soft, 15-20 minutes - this real charring is what gives baba ghanoush its smoky character.
Let cool slightly, then scoop out the flesh, discarding the charred skin.
Mash with the tahini, garlic, and lemon juice until well combined but still a little textured.
Drizzle with olive oil before serving.

name: Egyptian Hummus
description: Hummus, a smooth chickpea and tahini dip, is genuinely believed to have roots in Egypt among several claimed origins across the region - real depth comes from blending long enough that the chickpeas turn genuinely silky, not just coarsely mashed, and a good pour of real tahini rather than using it sparingly.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, canned, drained solids

ingredients.ingredient: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, canned, drained solids

steps_detailed: Blend the chickpeas, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and cumin with a splash of water, running the blender a full 2-3 minutes and scraping down the sides, until genuinely smooth and light, not just coarsely broken up.
Adjust the consistency with more water if needed, a tablespoon at a time.
Spread onto a plate and drizzle with the olive oil before serving.

name: Egyptian Roasted Chickpea Snack
description: Roasted chickpeas, tossed with real cumin and olive oil until deeply crisp, are a common Egyptian snack, real technique patting the chickpeas completely dry first, since any leftover moisture steams them instead of letting them crisp.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, canned, drained solids
ingredients_full.note: patted very dry with a towel

steps_detailed: Toss the well-dried chickpeas with the oil, cumin, and salt.
Spread in a single layer on a baking sheet, giving each chickpea room so they roast rather than steam.
Roast at 400F (200C) for 25-30 minutes, shaking the pan halfway through, until deeply golden and crisp all the way through.

name: Egyptian Cucumber Tomato Salad
description: A simple, bright cucumber and tomato salad, a common accompaniment across Egypt, real versions often finished with a scatter of fresh mint for real freshness against the acidity.
steps_detailed: Toss the cucumber and tomatoes with the lemon juice and olive oil.
Scatter the fresh mint over the top just before serving.

name: Egyptian Roasted Almonds
description: A simple roasted almond snack, common across Egypt, real technique toasting just until the almonds turn fragrant and lightly golden inside, not fully dark, since they'll continue cooking slightly off the heat.
steps_detailed: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, 4-5 minutes, until fragrant and lightly golden - watch closely, since they go from perfect to burnt quickly.
Toss with a pinch of salt while still warm.

name: Egyptian Mint Tea
description: Mint tea, sweetened black tea steeped with fresh mint, is central to Egyptian hospitality.
steps_detailed: Warm the tea with the torn mint 5 minutes, letting the leaves fully steep and bruise slightly to release their oils.
Stir in the sugar until fully dissolved.
Strain if desired before serving hot.

name: Egyptian Grilled Kofta
description: Kofta, spiced ground meat formed onto skewers and grilled, real depth coming from a proper mix of real parsley and warming spices worked into the meat, not just salt and pepper.
steps_detailed: Mix the beef with the grated onion, cilantro, cumin, and paprika until well combined.
Shape onto skewers or into small logs.
Grill, turning, 8-9 minutes, until charred and cooked through.

name: Egyptian Bamia
description: Bamia, okra stewed with meat and tomato until it thickens naturally, is a genuine Egyptian home-cooking staple, real technique searing the okra briefly before it goes into the stew, which helps it hold its shape rather than turning slimy.
steps_detailed: Sear the okra alone in the olive oil over medium-high heat, 3-4 minutes, until lightly browned - this real searing step helps it hold together rather than turning slimy in the stew.
Set the okra aside, then brown the beef with the garlic in the same pan, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Return the okra and simmer 6-8 minutes more until tender and the stew has thickened.

name: Egyptian Tahini Sauce
description: The real tahini sauce that accompanies falafel, grilled meats, and vegetables across Egypt, made here on its own for use in other dishes.
steps_detailed: Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, garlic, and enough water to reach a smooth, pourable consistency.

name: Egyptian Da'ah (Garlic Vinegar Sauce)
description: Da'ah, the sharp, uncooked garlic-vinegar sauce that defines real koshari, made here on its own - real da'ah is never cooked, which is what gives it its bright, punchy character against the tomato sauce's cooked depth.
steps_detailed: Whisk the garlic, vinegar, cumin, and a splash of water together.
Let sit at least 15 minutes so the flavors infuse - never cook this sauce.
